title: Jambavan Reminds Hanuman of His Strength
text:
In the Ramayana, the monkey army was searching the south for Sita, Rama's wife, who had been carried off by the demon king Ravana. At last they reached the shore of the ocean and learned that she was held in Lanka, an island a hundred leagues across the sea. Nobody could see how to get there.

The leaders gathered on the beach, and one after another they said how far they could leap. One could manage ten leagues, another twenty, another more. Prince Angada thought he could reach Lanka but was unsure he could return. None of them was enough. Through all this, Hanuman sat apart and said nothing.

The old bear Jambavan, the wisest of the company, went over to him. He reminded Hanuman who he was: the son of the wind god, a match for the eagle Garuda in speed. He reminded him how, as a child, he had leaped into the sky to grab the rising sun, thinking it was a ripe fruit. Why, Jambavan asked, was he sitting silent when he alone could do this?

As Hanuman listened, he began to grow. He climbed Mount Mahendra, gathered his strength, and with the army cheering below, sprang out over the ocean toward Lanka.
lesson: Sometimes the person a team needs most does not know their own ability. Reminding a colleague what they have already done can unlock what the whole group needs.
people: Jambavan, Hanuman, Angada, the monkey army
date: c. 5th century BC to 3rd century AD (text)
source: Valmiki, Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, cantos 65 to 67
